title: The flower and the robe
hookLine: tradition says the boy Har Rai brushed a flower with his robe, broke it, and was told to walk gently all his life

cards: You've probably done it. Rushing through a doorway with a bag on your shoulder and knocking a glass off the counter. Catching someone's elbow with your backpack on the train.

Walking through a garden and realizing, too late, that you've stepped on the one flower about to open. Nobody meant anything. You were just moving through the world a little too big, a little too fast.
Tradition says it happened once to a boy at Kiratpur, the grandson Guru Hargobind would choose as the next Guru, and that what his grandfather told him shaped the rest of his life.

teach.b: Here is the story as Sikhs tell it. The boy Har Rai was walking through the garden at Kiratpur in a long, flowing robe.

As he passed a flowering bush, the edge of his robe caught the flowers and broke them, and the petals fell to the ground. He stopped, upset. His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, saw it happen, and didn't scold him.
Tradition says he told him gently: if you wear a flowing robe, you must learn to carry it carefully, so it doesn't harm the things around you. The boy took it to heart.
For the rest of his life, it's said, Har Rai walked holding his robe close, careful of flowers. That's the whole story. It's tiny, and it turned into a way of life.

Har Rai became the seventh Guru, and Sikhs remember him above all for gentleness. He loved nature, and kept gardens and animals. Tradition says he kept horsemen, as his grandfather had, but never fought a battle.

Read the robe as a picture of whatever gives a person size in the world: strength, voice, money, position, even a mood that fills a room. In the story the robe stays on; the boy learns to carry it close.

teach.h: THE BIGGER THE ROBE, THE GENTLER.
teach.b: The bigger the robe, the more carefully he walks.
Sikhs see in the seventh Guru a picture of what power looks like when it is gentle.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, for his gentleness and love of nature, and the story of the flower and the robe is often told to children.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for one minute, across the room or outside, slower than feels normal, feeling each foot land, heel, then toe.
Notice how much room you take, your arms, your elbows, your bag, and move as if there were flowers on every side. Then sit, and let that gentleness settle into your breath.

wordCard.voice: Har Rai. The boy who broke a flower with his flowing robe at Kiratpur, and learned from his grandfather to walk gently for the rest of his life.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Har Rai, the name of the seventh Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: walk gently. A very small moment can shape a whole life. Nearly seventy days now.
